Rich is a Python library for _rich_ text and beautiful formatting in the terminal.

The [Rich API](https://rich.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) makes it easy to add color and style to terminal output. Rich can also render pretty tables, progress bars, markdown, syntax highlighted source code, tracebacks, and more — out of the box.

![Features](https://github.com/textualize/rich/raw/main/imgs/features.png)

For a video introduction to Rich see [calmcode.io](https://calmcode.io/rich/introduction.html) by [@fishnets88](https://twitter.com/fishnets88).

See what [people are saying about Rich](https://www.willmcgugan.com/blog/pages/post/rich-tweets/).

## Compatibility

Rich works with Linux, macOS and Windows. True color / emoji works with new Windows Terminal, classic terminal is limited to 16 colors. Rich requires Python 3.8 or later.

Rich works with [Jupyter notebooks](https://jupyter.org/) with no additional configuration required.

## Installing

Install with `pip` or your favorite PyPI package manager.

```sh
python -m pip install rich
```

Run the following to test Rich output on your terminal:

```sh
python -m rich
```

## Rich Print

To effortlessly add rich output to your application, you can import the [rich print](https://rich.readthedocs.io/en/latest/introduction.html#quick-start) method, which has the same signature as the builtin Python function. Try this:

```python
from rich import print

print("Hello, [bold magenta]World[/bold magenta]!", ":vampire:", locals())
```

![Hello World](https://github.com/textualize/rich/raw/main/imgs/print.png)

## Rich REPL

Rich can be installed in the Python REPL, so that any data structures will be pretty printed and highlighted.

```python
>>> from rich import pretty
>>> pretty.install()
```

![REPL](https://github.com/textualize/rich/raw/main/imgs/repl.png)

## Using the Console

For more control over rich terminal content, import and construct a [Console](https://rich.readthedocs.io/en/latest/reference/console.html#rich.console.Console) object.

```python
from rich.console import Console

console = Console()
```

The Console object has a `print` method which has an intentionally similar interface to the builtin `print` function. Here's an example of use:

```python
console.print("Hello", "World!")
```

As you might expect, this will print `"Hello World!"` to the terminal. Note that unlike the builtin `print` function, Rich will word-wrap your text to fit within the terminal width.

There are a few ways of adding color and style to your output. You can set a style for the entire output by adding a `style` keyword argument. Here's an example:

```python
console.print("Hello", "World!", style="bold red")
```

The output will be something like the following:

![Hello World](https://github.com/textualize/rich/raw/main/imgs/hello_world.png)

That's fine for styling a line of text at a time. For more finely grained styling, Rich renders a special markup which is similar in syntax to [bbcode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBCode). Here's an example:

```python
console.print("Where there is a [bold cyan]Will[/bold cyan] there [u]is[/u] a [i]way[/i].")
```

![Console Markup](https://github.com/textualize/rich/raw/main/imgs/where_there_is_a_will.png)

You can use a Console object to generate sophisticated output with minimal effort. See the [Console API](https://rich.readthedocs.io/en/latest/console.html) docs for details.

## Rich Inspect

Rich has an [inspect](https://rich.readthedocs.io/en/latest/reference/init.html?highlight=inspect#rich.inspect) function which can produce a report on any Python object, such as class, instance, or builtin.

```python
>>> my_list = ["foo", "bar"]
>>> from rich import inspect
>>> inspect(my_list, methods=True)
```

![Log](https://github.com/textualize/rich/raw/main/imgs/inspect.png)

See the [inspect docs](https://rich.readthedocs.io/en/latest/reference/init.html#rich.inspect) for details.

Based on the README at this pinned revision, here is how Rich presents terminal output.

## Summary

The README (source: https://github.com/Textualize/rich/blob/9d8f9a372cc5916fd4781fec207ced7ddac2f08f/README.md) describes Rich as "a Python library for _rich_ text and beautiful formatting in the terminal." Its stated purpose is that the "Rich API makes it easy to add color and style to terminal output," and it "can also render pretty tables, progress bars, markdown, syntax highlighted source code, tracebacks, and more — out of the box."

## How output is presented, per the README

**1. Entry points for producing output**
- **`rich.print`** — a drop-in replacement with "the same signature as the builtin Python function," supporting markup and emoji, e.g. `print("Hello, [bold magenta]World[/bold magenta]!", ":vampire:", locals())`.
- **Rich REPL** — via `from rich import pretty; pretty.install()`, so "any data structures will be pretty printed and highlighted."
- **`Console` object** — for "more control over rich terminal content," with a `print` method that has "an intentionally similar interface to the builtin `print` function."

**2. Styling and layout behavior**
- Unlike the builtin `print`, "Rich will word-wrap your text to fit within the terminal width."
- Whole-output styling via a `style` keyword, e.g. `console.print("Hello", "World!", style="bold red")`.
- Finer-grained styling uses "a special markup which is similar in syntax to bbcode," e.g. `[bold cyan]`, `[u]`, `[i]`.
- Emoji are inserted by placing a name between two colons (e.g. `:smiley: :vampire:`).

**3. Built-in renderables** (the README's "Rich Library" section, presented as collapsible `<details>` blocks)
- **Log** — `console.log()` adds "a column for the current time and the file and line which made the call," does syntax highlighting for Python structures and repr strings, and pretty-prints collections; `log_locals=True` outputs a table of local variables.
- **Logging Handler** — a builtin Handler class to "format and colorize output from Python's logging module."
- **Emoji** — colon-delimited emoji names.
- **Tables** — "flexible tables with unicode box characters," with options for borders, styles, and cell alignment; the `Table` class "is smart enough to resize columns to fit the available width of the terminal, wrapping text as required." Console markup works in tables, and "anything that is renderable by Rich may be included in the headers / rows (even other tables)."
- **Progress Bars** — "multiple flicker-free progress bars," via `track()` or configurable columns (percentage, file size, file speed, time remaining).
- **Status** — `console.status()` displays "a 'spinner' animation and message" without preventing normal console use.

**4. Compatibility / environment**
- Works on Linux, macOS, and Windows; "True color / emoji works with new Windows Terminal, classic terminal is limited to 16 colors." Requires Python 3.8+.
- "Rich works with Jupyter notebooks with no additional configuration required."

## Caveats / uncertainty
- The README file was truncated at ~12,000 characters in my retrieval, so the tail of the document (after the Status section) was not fully observed. The README's `<details>` sections continue beyond what I read, so additional renderables (e.g., markdown, syntax, tracebacks, trees, columns, panels, layout) are referenced in the intro but their detailed README sections were not captured here.
- The README is documentation/marketing material; it describes intended behavior rather than implementation details. I did not inspect the source code to verify each claim.

Evidence is drawn solely from `README.md` at ref `9d8f9a372cc5916fd4781fec207ced7ddac2f08f`.

**URL:** https://github.com/encode/httpx/issues/895
**State:** Closed | **Label:** question | **Opened:** 2020-04-05 by `mengyyy`

### The reported cookie persistence problem

The user was trying to **save cookies to a pickle file and reload them into a new `httpx.Client`**. The workflow was:

1. Save cookies by iterating `client.cookies.items()` into a plain dict and pickling it.
2. Load them back via `httpx.Client(cookies=load_cookies())` — this worked once.
3. But **re-saving** (iterating `client.cookies.items()` again) raised a `CookieConflict` exception:

```
CookieConflict: Multiple cookies exist with name=ipb_coppa
```

Inspecting `client.cookies.keys()` revealed **duplicate cookie names**:
```
['ipb_coppa', 'ipb_member_id', 'ipb_pass_hash', 'ipb_session_id',
 'ipb_member_id', 'ipb_pass_hash', 'ipb_session_id', 'ipb_coppa']
```

### Root cause (identified in the discussion)

- **`oczkers`** pinpointed the mechanism: importing cookies from a plain dict sets the cookie **domain to an empty string**, whereas the server sets cookies **with a real domain**. This produces two cookies with the same name — one domain-less (from the dict) and one domain-scoped (from the server). Iterating `.items()` then hits `CookieConflict` because `Cookies.get()` finds multiple matches for the same name.
- A minimal repro confirmed it: after `client.get(...)` sets `key=value` (domain `httpbin.org`), calling `r.cookies.update({'key': 'value2'})` adds a second `key` cookie with `domain=''`, yielding duplicates.

### Maintainer position

- **`florimondmanca`** argued the `CookieConflict` is **legitimate behavior**, since cookies are domain-sensitive and the user was reusing session-sensitive cookies across sessions. He recommended using `httpx.Cookies` and its `.set()` method (which allows specifying domain/path), and suggested pickling the `CookieJar` object directly to retain domain info.

### Workarounds shared in the thread

- Pickle `client.cookies.jar` directly (maintainer's suggestion).
- **`mengyyy`**: pickle `client.cookies.jar._cookies` and rebuild via `cookies.set(k, v.value, domain=domain, path=path)`.
- **`septatrix`** noted the `CookieJar` approach fails because **`CookieJar` has a non-picklable lock**.
- **`aeryncaen`**: pickle `Client.cookies.jar._cookies`, then `Client.cookies.jar._cookies.update(loaded_cookies)`, followed by `clear_expired_cookies()`.
- **`realsuayip`** (2025): a JSON serialization helper iterating `cookies.jar` and extracting cookie attributes.

### Conclusion

The reported problem is a **cookie persistence / round-trip issue**: saving cookies as a plain name→value dict loses domain (and path) information, so reloading them into a new client creates domain-less duplicates that collide with server-set domain-scoped cookies, triggering `CookieConflict` on subsequent iteration. The maintainers considered the conflict itself correct behavior and pointed to domain-aware APIs (`Cookies.set`, pickling the jar) as the proper fix. The issue was closed as a question.
